newsitem.title: USA: Dollar hurt by Hashimoto comment, drop in Dow.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hurt by Hashimoto comment, drop in Dow.

text.p: The dollar fell against the yen on Monday after remarks from Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto tying exchange rate stability to Japan's holdings of U.S. Treasuries sent U.S. stocks tumbling.

Hashimoto, answering questions after delivering a speech to investors at Columbia University in New York, said: "I hope the U.S. will engage in efforts and in cooperation to maintain exchange (rate) stability so we will not succumb to the temptation to sell off Treasury bills and switch our funds to gold."

His remarks triggered the second-largest single-day point drop in the history of the Dow Jones industrial average, which plummeted 192.25 points to 7,604.26, trailing only the 508-point Black Monday market crash of Oct. 19, 1987.
U.S. Treasuries bonds were also weighed down by Hashimoto's remark.

The dollar closed at 114.93 yen, well below its session high of 115.67 yen reached overnight after a weekend summit of industrialised nations played down U.S.-Japan trade concerns, buoying the U.S. currency. However, the dollar ended nearly unchanged from Friday's 114.85 close.
Despite the flurry of dollar trading in late U.S. trading, a sharp rally in the British pound dominated most of the session's activity, traders said.
The pound continued a rally started on Friday and shot up to its highest level since Jan. 16 versus the dollar and its peak since July 1992 against the mark.

"Sterling's benefited from a combination of events ranging from a safe haven from European Economic and Monetary Union to the outlook for higher rates," said Bob Near, vice president and trader at the Bank of New York.
Recent UK economic data suggest the Bank of England may raise official interest rates for a third time this cycle to keep inflation in check. The rate hike could come as early as July, dealers said.
"It looks like the pressure is on the Bank of England to raise rates," said Ron Leven, currency strategist at JP Morgan in New York.
Against the German mark and most other major European currencies, the dollar edged lower as activity focused on the yen and pound.
The dollar slipped to 1.7185 marks at the close from 1.7287 at the end of business Friday and to 1.4320 Swiss francs from 1.4403. Sterling jumped to $1.6715 from $1.6560.
In other trading, the dollar was unchanged at Canadian $1.3885.
Dealers were relieved the G7 leaders did not mention specific currency levels or concerns over dollar strength.

"There were no major signs of tension; no mention at all about currency levels and no indication at all that there were concerns about dollar strength," Leven said. "If anything, the comments seemed to point to stability at these levels."
At the Denver summit, President Bill Clinton warned Japan that an explosive deterioration in the U.S.-Japan balance of trade could endanger the relationship between the two economic powerhouses.

Japan reported last week that its trade surplus tripled in May from a year earlier. U.S. officials are worried that the rise is the start of a steady climb in the surplus back to levels that in the past have led to trade friction.
But Hashimoto blamed the rising surplus on temporary factors and said he did not expect it to continue to climb significantly.
